item.text: {"verdicts":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E001","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E002","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E003","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports Pegasus espionage against a human-rights defender and two journalists during the current administration, including military surveillance; it states that the president denied the reports and that official resources were used for a campaign to contest them. It also says accountability for the military's digital-security and surveillance failures had not been addressed.","notes":["The excerpt does not use the broader wording 'documented Pegasus espionage against human-rights defenders and journalists' beyond the named cases.","'No effective accountability' is narrowed to the report's statement that accountability was not discussed/addressed."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E004","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E005","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E006","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports that beneficiaries of Sembrando Vida and Benito Juárez scholarships faced insufficient information and training, digital-access barriers, weak monitoring, travel burdens, and payment irregularities. It cites Coneval's finding that Sembrando Vida's operating rules did not define selection or prioritization mechanisms or the programmed-target concept, and cites reporting of unexplained Benito Juárez payments.","notes":["The excerpt supports these documented barriers and cited findings, but not the broader characterization that both programs 'reached millions' as a central fact of this excerpt.","The payment figures are reported through cited external sources, not independently established by ARTICLE 19."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E007","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E008","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 documents 696 attacks against the press and 12 journalist killings in 2022, with public officials as the largest identified perpetrator category in its breakdown and organized-crime involvement reported in some cases. It reports that the ten media companies receiving the most federal communication resources received 54.8% of the total, and describes official discourse and discretionary advertising as forms of direct or indirect censorship.","notes":["The excerpt supports 195 attacks attributed to public officials, not the phrase 'state actors as the largest identified perpetrator category' without that qualification.","The excerpt reports organized-crime presence or involvement, not necessarily 'criminal-group presence across much of the country' as a general causal premise."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E009","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E010","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E011","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E012","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E013","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E014","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports that the federal victim commission lacked a titular head for a year and a half and had insufficient budget growth; the National Victim System had met only once in almost ten years; military budgets substantially exceeded civil security and justice budgets; and government discourse portrayed victims as seeking benefits. It also reports a November 2022 official meeting at which the government reaffirmed a commitment to strengthen victim services and announced the system's reinstatement.","notes":["The excerpt supports 'without a titular head' and budget limitations, not necessarily 'vacant or underfunded' as a general characterization.","The announced plan is not evidence that victim attention was actually strengthened."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E015","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 reports that 25 high-level public appointments were pending or delayed in the described 2022 accounting, of which only five were filled, leaving 20 unresolved at the end of 2022. It reports that Cofece lacked a quorum because of uncompleted appointments and that the Supreme Court ordered the Executive to submit three pending Cofece proposals.","notes":["The excerpt does not support the summary's statement that all listed bodies were 'impaired or at risk of lacking quorum'; it specifically states that Cofece lacked the quorum needed for full functions and separately discusses IFT and Inai risks."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E016","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E017","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E018","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E019","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E020","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19's agenda proposes reforms concerning discretionary official advertising, criminal speech restrictions, journalist protection, institutional coordination, and official stigmatization; its inclusion of these proposals identifies issues the organization seeks to address.","notes":["The excerpt is an agenda of proposed measures and does not by itself establish that all of the corresponding reforms remained outstanding at publication."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E021","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19's agenda proposes transparent appointment processes, judicial authorization or review for content-removal and surveillance requests, transparency concerning Pegasus-related contracting, independent investigations, anti-impunity measures, safeguards against digital censorship, and inclusive connectivity.","notes":["The excerpt supports proposed safeguards and reforms, but their inclusion does not by itself establish that every corresponding institutional risk was present or that every safeguard was absent in practice."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E022","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"ARTICLE 19 recommends culturally appropriate proactive information, disaster-prevention planning, transparent appointments, autonomous information institutions, and accountability for protest-related abuses. It identifies digital and linguistic barriers for Indigenous communities and calls for better coordination among authorities and affected groups.","notes":["The excerpt is primarily a set of recommendations; it does not independently establish that all named communities lacked adequate information or participation, or that institutions were generally insufficiently coordinated."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0018-E023","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]}]}
